title: Passkeys vs passwords: what actually changes?
description: Passkeys replace a shared secret with a pair of cryptographic keys. Here's why that makes phishing and password leaks far less useful to attackers.

scenes.say: What if there was no password for a hacker to steal? That's the idea behind passkeys.
A password is a secret you hand to the website, so anyone who learns it can use it. With a passkey, your device holds a private key, and the site keeps only the matching public key.
Logging in goes like this. The site sends a random challenge. Your device signs it, after you approve with a fingerprint, face or PIN. Nothing reusable crosses the internet.

scenes.sub: a fake page gets nothing usable
scenes.say: Each passkey is tied to the real website, so a lookalike phishing page can't trigger a login. That's why passkeys resist phishing.

steps: Keep your device backup switched on
scenes.say: To try one, open your account's security settings and create a passkey. Keep your backup on, so you don't get locked out. Follow for the next one.
